scope: Checked against the eight scholarly articles, news report, teacher opinion and workplace guidance read for the November 16–22 publication window. Claims and limits are identified at each cited passage.

source_locator: Limitations inherited from the primary literature
checks: Researchers coded 93 higher-education studies for the work students delegated, their responses to AI output and evidence of learning without assistance. They distinguished reported behavior from inferences based on the assignment design.

Eighty-five studies identified delegated tasks, 44 described how students responded to AI and 24 measured learning without AI. Only four documented both responses and independent learning. One learner rejected a suggestion that conflicted with the terminology in their own text.
Half of the 44 studies describing responses relied on self-reports or author summaries. Follow-up was too short to assess cumulative effects.

checks: The authors pooled correlations from 31 studies involving 16,357 participants. Their model estimated how AI use related to critical thinking through two reported experiences, learning motivation and dependence on AI.

The estimated indirect associations ran in opposite directions. The motivation pathway was +0.217 and the dependence pathway was −0.212. Their sum was close to zero (reported estimate 0.004, p = .645). The adjusted direct association between use and critical thinking was positive (0.149).
Most included studies measured people at a single point in time. The model cannot establish which experience came first.

source_locator: Research methodology, measures of practice intensity
Results, Practice intensity, Table 2 and Figure 4
checks: Thirty business undergraduates in Germany practiced with a GPT exam assistant during one course unit and Moodle quizzes during the next. The researchers examined 224 assistant launches, course activity and student surveys.

Students answered the opening question in about half of assistant launches. Roughly 40% of launches ended with completion of the entire exercise, including a case study. Reported practice times were similar in both units. Most respondents preferred Moodle for future graded assignments.
One class used the formats in a fixed order with different subject matter. Moodle lacked comparable question-level traces, and the design could not isolate learning differences.

source_locator: What UnBlooms Looks Like in Practice
checks: Austin, Gulya and Kassorla examine how generative AI changes the relationship between a finished assignment and the thinking it once signaled. They compare learning frameworks and illustrate their proposed approach through a hypothetical biochemistry class. The class begins with an AI-generated explanation. Groups identify assumptions and errors in the explanation and accompanying image. A learner who lacks background knowledge can research a claim before assessing it. A classmate with that knowledge can challenge it immediately.

The authors suggest letting students move repeatedly between evaluation, background reading and revision. The reasons a student gives for retaining or changing an AI suggestion become material for assessment.
The authors use the class to illustrate their framework. They report no classroom observations or comparison of learning outcomes.

Matsui draws on journal policies and earlier studies of disclosure to develop a theory of how readers allocate attention when an author reports using AI. The paper distinguishes scrutiny that addresses a research decision from scrutiny prompted by an AI label alone. If AI contributed to an analysis, checking the code is relevant. If a writer reports grammar correction, hunting for familiar AI phrasing could draw attention away from the evidence.

Matsui proposes giving readers identical manuscripts with different descriptions of editing. Reading time, comments and comprehension could help distinguish a change in where readers look from a change in how much they trust the author.
The article proposes this experiment. It reports no reader-attention data.

checks: Kearney develops a framework for interpreting AI-assisted assignments and applies it to a hypothetical 2,000-word case analysis. It asks who made the important decisions and what evidence of those decisions an instructor can inspect. In one version, a student submits every exchange but accepts each AI suggestion unquestioningly. In another, the student weighs competing interpretations but submits only the final answer. Both leave the instructor with difficulties in judging capability, for different reasons.

Kearney suggests asking students to annotate their responses to objections or orally defend two interpretive choices. Either can expose the reasoning behind a case analysis. The relevant evidence depends on the capability the assignment is intended to certify.
The examples illustrate possible designs. Their effects on learning, later transfer and grading workload need empirical tests.

sources.source_locator: Original CPR News article, sections “Students and AI” and “Teachers and AI,” especially Donjuan’s revision example and Wilson’s account of classroom writing.
checks: In Colorado classrooms, the choice of when to introduce AI shapes which parts of writing students still practice themselves.

Marissa Donjuan asked AI to compare an essay she had written with her teacher’s comments and rubric. At the University of Denver, Josh Wilson moved extended writing into class so he could see students develop their arguments.
These classroom accounts establish what participants tried. Their effects on learning and attention remain unmeasured.

sources.source_locator: Full EdSurge essay, including the opening account of the proposed lesson, “Pulling Back the Tech” and “Ready for the Future.”
checks: Court Shuller makes a case for reserving the language arts period for reading, writing and discussion, even as the teacher pursues professional training in AI.

Shuller designed a lesson in which students would compare their vocabulary maps with AI-generated ones. The lesson stayed on paper. Daily classroom activities instead include handwritten first drafts and discussion of texts.
Shuller’s observations concern a wider switch away from laptops. They cannot isolate an effect of AI on attention or comprehension.

sources.source_locator: Full report, objectives 4 (Job design) and 5 (Expertise), especially the suggested practices, examples and warning signs. Date verified on APA’s report page and release.
checks: An employer assigning people to oversee AI also needs to give them time to check its work and opportunities to develop the judgment that checking requires.
The guide flags reviews pushed beyond working hours as a sign of uncounted effort. It suggests that employees learning a task try it before consulting the tool, then compare the approaches.
APA identifies long-standing evidence about attention and skill acquisition and emerging evidence about how much verification work AI creates or how it changes professional learning.

Researchers linked questionnaires from 1,461 students aged 12–17 at urban Chinese schools to fitness tests and standardized scores in Chinese, mathematics and English. The questionnaires measured reliance on generative AI and students' reported ability to direct their attention.

Students who reported greater dependence on AI also reported poorer attentional control and had lower academic scores. Statistical models linked dependence to scores through attentional control and fitness, separately and in combination.
The measures came from one period. Students rated their own attention. The study did not track when they sought AI help or control for family socioeconomic circumstances.

Jia surveyed 1,050 university students with experience using generative AI. They reported tasks delegated to it, their mental effort and their engagement with coursework. The analysis accounted for task categories, including fact retrieval and outlining.

Reported delegation had no clear overall linear relationship with engagement. The model linked offloading with lower engagement through extraneous demands such as checking answers, and with higher engagement through effort spent understanding the material. Differences between memory-related and analytical offloading were statistically inconclusive.
All measures were self-reports collected at one time. The study included neither a memory test nor observations of what learners verified.
